newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN urges Iraq to admit 1,320 Turkish Kurd refugees.
newsitem.headline: UN urges Iraq to admit 1,320 Turkish Kurd refugees.

text.p: The United Nations refugee agency called on Iraq on Friday to allow some 1,320 displaced Turkish Kurds to enter its territory.
Spokesman Kris Janowski said the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) would ask Baghdad to register and screen them to determine their legal status.

Nearly 2,000 Turkish Kurds have left the troubled Atrush camp in northern Iraq since mid-February. Some 1,320 are now in Ain Sufni, on the edge of a zone controlled by the Iraqi government just south of the area ruled by Iraqi Kurdish rebels.
The refugees have said they moved to Ain Sufni, 100 km (60 miles) from the Turkish border, to seek Iraqi protection from Turkish attacks.

In January, UNHCR withdrew from Atrush camp, which Turkey says is a base for guerrillas of the independence-seeking Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK), saying Kurdish rebels among the refugees were blocking its aid work.
"We are pleased that an increasing number of refugees are leaving Atrush camp... enabling us to provide assistance to them individually or in smaller groups," Janowski told a news briefing.

Referring to the 1,320 in Ain Sufni, he said: "Through our office in Baghdad, UNHCR is officially requesting the government of Iraq to let these refugees enter its territory so that they can be properly sheltered and assisted.
"Upon entering the government areas we will request that the refugees be properly screened and registered so that the civilian character will be maintained at the new site."
UNHCR pulled out of Atrush on January 21 after repeated calls from Turkey for the separation of rebels from refugees and the closure of the camp.

Atrush, 60 km (38 miles) from the Turkish border, was set up in 1994 for Kurds fleeing into northern Iraq from south-east Turkey, where villagers are caught in the middle of a war between Turkish troops and the PKK.
More than 21,000 people have died in the 12-year-old conflict.
